description: Matías Navarro, fundador de ORA IA (Chile). Mención Best AI Builder, Claude Impact Lab 2026. Abordamos veinte años de detecciones satelitales de fuego repartidas entre sensores que no se pueden comparar. Buscamos experiencia en teledetección, SIG o productos de fuego activo; también análisis de datos o desarrollo web. Lidero la coordinación. Trabajamos en español, entregamos en inglés.
summary: Overlap turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS fire hotspots from two generations of satellites into one honest, comparable record for Chile. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fire very differently: in the Biobío region, VIIRS records about 5.9 times more hotspots than MODIS Aqua over the complete fire seasons 2012–13 to 2025–26, so joining them as they are invents an almost fivefold jump in 2012. We harmonize MODIS into Suomi NPP-equivalent units with quantile maps calibrated on the 2012–2026 overlap, and we show how much to trust every number. Against 76,002 CONAF fire records in the four calibrated regions, the false jump falls from ×4.7 to ×0.89 (95% CI 0.77–1.07: no jump). The result is a free bilingual web app where a fire-prevention analyst can see, in seconds, whether this month and this season are unusual for their region, and where in the region the hotspots fall. This matters now: MODIS ends in 2027 and Suomi NPP stopped delivering new data on November 2, 2026, so the long record only survives if it can be stitched together honestly.
details:
The problem

Satellites have tracked active fires for 25 years, but the record is split between MODIS (1 km pixels, Terra from 2000 and Aqua from 2002) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, from 2012). VIIRS sees many more small fires, so any long series that joins both shows a jump in 2012 that is the sensor, not the fire.

Our user is the fire-prevention analyst (for example, CONAF in Biobío) preparing the season, who needs to know whether this month and this season are unusual compared with the past.

What it does

The app shows, for Chile, any of its 16 regions or the historical Biobío region:

  • Headline status: the latest month against the same month in every previous season (robust z on a log scale), labelled as provisional when it comes from near real-time data.
  • This season so far against every past season, in plain language, with scenarios (not forecasts) for how it could end.
  • 25-year calendar of harmonized hotspots, month × year, with a Raw/Harmonized switch that shows the 2012 jump appear and disappear.
  • The 2012 jump, before and after harmonization, with the CONAF result for the selected area.
  • Animated map of Chile, region by region, that plays 25 years month by month and zooms into a region’s communes to show where its hotspots fall.
  • Go to any coordinate: the app finds its region and commune and the nearest hotspot of the month; every hotspot is drawn as its satellite pixel, to scale.
  • Season clock that shows whether the busiest time of the fire season is shifting (a shift counts only if it also appears in the VIIRS-only years), a day-by-day view of any month, and a trust table with the measured error and the CONAF result for every region.
  • Open downloads: CSV (monthly series and hotspot points with pixel-centre coordinates), GeoPackage and GeoJSON (ready for the QGIS Temporal Controller), shareable links, English and Spanish, and a colour-blind safe palette.

How it works

  1. Data: FIRMS archive files for MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m Collection 2 (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), science-quality data to July 2026 and near real-time data to November 7, 2026. We keep presumed vegetation fires (FIRMS type 0), drop low-confidence detections and assign each hotspot to its commune and region with the BCN boundaries.
  2. One unit: everything is expressed as the hotspots one VIIRS satellite (Suomi NPP) would record; satellites are never summed.
  3. Harmonization: monthly quantile mapping on log(1 + hotspots), fitted where both sensors observed (2012–2026): one map per region and sensor in Maule, Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía; a pooled map in nine other regions; a simple ratio in Los Ríos, Los Lagos and Aysén, where the pooled map did worse.

Validation: measured, not assumed

  • Against the ground: checked with 76,002 CONAF fire records in the four calibrated regions, the false 2012 jump falls from ×4.7 to ×0.89 (95% CI 0.77–1.07: no jump).
  • On hidden years (fit 2012–2019, test 2020–2026): quantile mapping beats a simple ratio in all four calibrated regions (mean monthly error ×1.47; median ×1.33), and the pooled map beats each region’s own ratio in 9 of 12 other regions.
  • All of Chile: against 109,947 CONAF fires (2002–2020), the false jump disappears in 9 of the 11 regions with enough fires. The app flags Valparaíso (overcorrected), Metropolitana (undercorrected), and the north and Magallanes, where CONAF has too few fires to judge. For Chile as a whole part of the jump remains (×4.41 → ×1.33, 95% CI 1.18–1.49), mostly from Metropolitana, and the app shows it.
  • Large fires: in the historical Biobío region (Biobío and Ñuble), MODIS Aqua detected 88% of the large fires (≥ 200 ha) of 2002–2020 and VIIRS 97% of those of 2012–2020 (a hotspot within 3 km, from 1 day before to 2 days after the start).

Honesty by design

Every estimated month carries an 80% range, provisional months are marked, months without a record are shown as no data (never zero), and recent near real-time months over the Atacama desert are withheld because of daytime false detections.

Benefits and intended impact

One comparable 25-year baseline per region, so a season can be judged against history instead of against a sensor change, with clear limits for every number. Fire-prevention teams in Chile can plan earlier. The code is open and the outputs use open formats that agencies and researchers can reuse, and the pipeline can be re-run for other countries covered by FIRMS, with their own calibration and ground truth.

Code and data: https://github.com/contactomtingcl/overlap

Creativity

Instead of hiding the sensor change, the app makes it visible: a Raw/Harmonized switch shows the 2012 jump appear and disappear, and every number says how far to trust it. We test the result against something the satellites never saw (fire records on the ground), not only against the satellites themselves.

Factors we considered

  • Satellites are never summed: the unit is one VIIRS satellite.
  • Months without data are never shown as zero; near real-time months are marked provisional.
  • Regions where the method fails against CONAF are flagged, not hidden.
  • Plain language for non-specialists, English and Spanish, and a colour-blind safe palette.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy) for the data pipeline · R (qmap, data.table) for the statistical models · a static web app in plain JavaScript and SVG on GitHub Pages · mapshaper for the boundaries · automated data checks and Playwright browser tests.

Next steps

Own quantile maps for Valparaíso and Metropolitana, a daily day/night model, GOES geostationary data to fill the hours between polar overpasses, burned-area checks with Landsat and Sentinel-2, context layers (vegetation, soil moisture, rainfall anomalies) and alerts to the responsible agency.

Use of AI

We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant to write and review most of the code of the data pipeline and the web app, to draft documentation and these texts, and to audit results for consistency. The team chose the challenge, the user and the method, designed and ran the statistical models in R, reviewed every result against the data, and made the decisions. Files written with AI assistance say so in their header, and docs/AI_USE.md describes it.

Demo video: the animations, motion graphics and the Overlap logo were made with AI assistance by filming the real web app with real NASA FIRMS data, and every AI-generated scene carries a visible “AI-generated” watermark. AI-generated audio: the background music was made with Suno and the sound effects were generated with Claude. The drone footage of the Universidad de Concepción campus was filmed by the team, and the voice-over was recorded by a team member, not generated. No AI-generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
